title: Reform Judaism
hookLine: ethics and informed personal choice at the center; tradition as a guide

lines: THREE BOOKS AND A COLD MUG.
cards: What would you keep, if nobody required it of you? A man sits at a kitchen table with three books open and a mug going cold. He grew up lighting candles on Friday night because his mother did.
Now he has his own kitchen, and nobody is going to check. So he is reading: what the Torah says about Shabbat, what the rabbis said, what his own congregation teaches.
By the end of the evening he hasn't decided everything. But the candles stay, and he knows why. Today, the movement that puts that kitchen table at the center.

teach.b: Reform Judaism. Bring back the three questions from earlier in this block: revelation, how binding halakha is, and how change happens. Here are Reform's answers, the way the movement describes itself.
First, ethics at the center. For Reform Jews, the heart of the Torah is its moral teaching: justice, honesty, care for the stranger and the poor. Those commandments are not optional.
Second, revelation keeps going. God's will is not only something given once, but something each generation keeps understanding, so the tradition can grow. Third, today's line: informed choice.
Rituals like Shabbat, the dietary laws and daily prayer are treated as a guide, not as binding law. Each Jew is asked to study them, then decide what to take on. The word informed matters.
It isn't do whatever you like.
It's learn first, then choose, exactly what the man at the kitchen table is doing.

Some Reform teachers point to a line from Deuteronomy, where Moses sets the choice before the people: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." A choice, made with eyes open.

Other movements weigh this differently. Orthodox Jews hold halakha as binding; Conservative Jews hold it as binding and developing. Reform places the decision in the hands of the person who has studied.
Three answers, three serious ways to hold one tradition.

how: Reform Jews treat the Torah's ethical commandments as central and approach ritual as a guide: individuals and congregations study practices like Shabbat, kashrut and prayer, then choose which to observe.

o: a movement that treats ritual as a guide you study and choose
a plan to update the old language of the Hebrew prayer book
a movement that keeps every law but shortens the services

s: informed choice means do whatever you like
the word informed matters: Reform asks Jews to study a practice first, then decide.
for Reform Jews, the Torah's ethical commandments are optional
ethics are at the center; it is ritual that is treated as a guide.
Reform teaches that revelation keeps going
each generation keeps understanding God's will, so the tradition can grow.

games.q: you've moved into your own place. nobody will check whether you light Shabbat candles. what do you do?
o: keep it because your mother did, and don't ask why.
study what it means, then decide.
games.why: the man at the kitchen table reads the Torah, the rabbis and his congregation's teaching first. the candles stay, and now he knows why. that is informed choice.

practice: Bring to mind one habit you keep without thinking: a word you say, a meal you skip, a ritual from your family or your own life. Ask three questions, slowly: where did this come from, what is it for, do I still want it?
You don't need to change anything; just know why you keep it, or why you'd let it go.

wordCard.voice: Reform Judaism. The movement that puts ethics at the center, sees revelation as ongoing, and treats ritual as a guide each Jew studies and then chooses from. Today's word.
